title: Domesticated forms vary more among individuals than wild species do

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Domesticated forms vary more among individuals than wild species do

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Individuals of the same variety of long-cultivated plants and domesticated animals generally differ much more from each other than individuals of any one species or variety in nature.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: they generally differ much more from each other, than do the individuals of any one species or variety in a state of nature.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter I, “Variation under Domestication”; section “Causes of Variability”. Scope: older cultivated plants and domesticated animals compared with wild species

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch01-01: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.70

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The comparison is direct and standard, and substantial public domestic data exist. Matched individual-level wild data across plants and animals are incomplete, limiting the stated breadth.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare within-population phenotypic or genomic variance in matched domesticated and wild taxa using common trait scales and hierarchical models. Greater variance across most matched pairs supports the generalization; equal or lower domestic variance refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Management populations and wild populations are not sampled comparably.

Trait choice strongly affects variance.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.74
analysis feasibility: 0.66
data existence: 0.72
operationalizability: 0.88
data adequacy: 0.49

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The comparison itself maps cleanly onto within-group dispersion, and public variant archives plus breed lists cover the main livestock and crop species. A full phenotypic test of older cultivated varieties against wild relatives still has to be compiled from studies and gene banks. The contrast can discriminate the stated pattern from its opposite for that subset, with the caveat that today's uniform breeds are a biased sample of what Darwin observed.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare within-variety coefficients of variation, or genomic heterozygosity, for homologous characters in long-cultivated populations and in wild populations of the parent species. Greater within-group dispersion in the domestic samples would support the contrast; equal or smaller domestic dispersion across a pre-registered trait set would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Genetic heterozygosity and visible individual differences can move in opposite directions after a domestication bottleneck.

Modern breed standards have deliberately reduced within-breed differences since the nineteenth century.

Individual-level phenotypic measurements are scattered, while public sequence archives over-represent a few commercial species.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.42
discriminating power: 0.62
analysis feasibility: 0.45
data existence: 0.55
operationalizability: 0.78
